passage:
Okay, so, I'm Nilesh, and the interviewer asked me, "What was the worst part?" Honestly, it wasn't the rumour itself. It was the three weeks of waiting. Somebody in the pantry said, "Cuts are coming to our division," and after that I did the rent maths every night. My EMI, my parents' expectation, my sister's fees. Tarun, my flatmate, found me at the table at 1 am with a calculator.

I could have panicked. I nearly typed an angry post about management. Instead I did the boring things. I moved a little from each salary into a separate account. I updated my resume on a Sunday and quietly messaged two old colleagues. And I kept doing my work well, because I still had it.

Tarun said, "You look like you're planning, not drowning." Some days I was doing both, I'll admit. But planning helped. 🙂

qa.q: What did Nilesh say was the worst part of the layoff rumour?
qa.a: Nilesh said the worst part was the three weeks of waiting after someone in the pantry said cuts were coming.

qa.q: What was Nilesh worried about at the table at 1 am?
qa.a: Nilesh was worried about rent, the EMI, family expectations and a sister's fees, and was doing the maths with a calculator.

qa.q: What did Nilesh do instead of panicking?
qa.a: Nilesh set aside a small buffer each month, updated the resume, quietly messaged two old colleagues and kept doing good work.

qa.q: How does Tarun see Nilesh's state during this time?
qa.a: Tarun sees someone who looks like a planner rather than someone drowning, though Nilesh admits to sometimes doing both at once.

grounding: Nilesh fears rumoured layoffs because of rent, EMIs and family, and responds by building a buffer, updating the resume and continuing to work.

passage:
Employee support note, Thursday 11 a.m.
Chetan came in after the rumour that the Pune office would cut a third of the team. He was pale and kept checking his phone. He said his rent is due, he pays an EMI on his sister's education loan, and his parents have told relatives about his "good IT job". He could not sleep. He asked if he should resign now, "before they fire me", or copy client files "just in case".
I told him the fear made sense, and that panic moves often hurt more. We wrote a list: update his resume this week, message three former colleagues, keep doing solid work, and not take any files. For money worries, I gave him the number of the free financial counselling line our office offers, so a qualified adviser can go through his options.
He left calmer. His wife, Deepika, will join him for the next session. Follow up Monday.

qa.q: What two things did Chetan ask about doing?
qa.a: Whether to resign now before being fired, or copy client files just in case.

qa.q: What was Chetan feeling when he came in, and how can you tell?
qa.a: He felt dread and panic about rent, the loan EMI and family expectations; he was pale, kept checking his phone and could not sleep.

qa.q: What steps did the note suggest instead of panic decisions?
qa.a: Updating his resume, quietly contacting three former colleagues, keeping up solid work, taking no files, and calling the free financial counselling line.

qa.q: How might Deepika be affected by the layoff rumour?
qa.a: Deepika may be anxious too, worried about the household and about Chetan's sleeplessness, which is why joining the next session helps.

grounding: Layoff rumours bring dread about rent, loans and family expectations; the protagonist is guided to prepare quietly, keep performing, and avoid panic or sabotage.

passage:
Sahil's diary, Wed 9 Oct.
Town hall today. "Restructuring." Nobody said the word layoff, but everyone heard it. My hands were cold all afternoon.
Rent, the phone EMI, and Maa already telling Nani I'm "settled". I kept thinking, what if I'm on the list?
Akash came to my desk at lunch and said, "Want to rage-quit with me?" Half joking. For a second I wanted to.
Instead, tonight:
- Updated my resume. First time in two years. Embarrassing but done.
- Messaged Priya from my old team to ask if her company is hiring.
- Stopped eating out this month. Asked Mama, who's a bank officer, to help me look over my savings plan properly this Sunday.
- Tomorrow I finish the Delhi report, on time, properly. Whatever happens, I want them to remember that.
Still scared. But less stuck.

qa.q: Who did Sahil message from the old team?
qa.a: Priya, to ask if her company is hiring.

qa.q: What was Sahil feeling after the town hall, and what shows it?
qa.a: Sahil felt scared and full of dread, with cold hands all afternoon and thoughts about rent and the EMI.

qa.q: How did Sahil avoid a panic decision?
qa.a: Sahil turned down the rage-quit, updated the resume, reached out quietly, cut back spending, asked a qualified family member for help with savings, and kept working well.

qa.q: How might Akash be feeling when he jokes about rage-quitting?
qa.a: Akash is probably just as frightened, hiding the fear behind a joke about quitting together.

grounding: Layoff rumours bring dread; the protagonist updates the resume, networks quietly, seeks proper help with money, keeps performing, and avoids a panic exit.
